Hyperboloid

GeometryCurvesCoordinates
Game: Straight bars join two round rings, and turning one ring bends them into a curved shape.
How to play: Slide the controls, drag the dot on the track, or press a shape button. Tick Solid to see the surface between the bars.
0 steps, 0.0° 25
Look for the math

The applet starts as a plain cylinder, yet its bars never bend. Only the places where they touch the top ring move. Here is what that does, and what the original page means by its curved surface.

What the page claims

The original page says: “At the outset, the applet below displays a cylinder, i.e., a prism. The edges joining the points on different bases are called generators. ... The result of the rotations is the 3D figure known as the one sheet hyperboloid. This same figure could be obtained by rotating a hyperbola around one of its axes of symmetry; just choose the one that does not intersect the hyperbola.” The logic test checked all 40 allowed numbers of lines against all 101 base shifts (4,040 settings): the start is a cylinder, every bar joins the two bases, and every point of every bar lies on the surface described below.

Two rings and their bars

The applet puts N equally spaced points on each ring, of radius R = 0.5, at heights ±L/2 with L = 1.5. Generator i runs from bottom point i to top point i + M, counting round the ring. So M is a number of steps, and the real turn is

φ = 2π (M mod N) / N

With M = 0 the bars stand straight: a cylinder. The Base Shift spinner goes to 100 even when N is as small as 5, so after a whole turn the picture starts again. The solid fill is always see-through in the applet, and turning Solid off switches Generators back on: both details are kept here.

The narrowest circle

Write t for the fraction of the way up a bar, so its height is y = (2t − 1)L/2. Adding the two ring coordinates gives the distance from the axis:

r² = R² [cos²(φ/2) + (2y/L)² sin²(φ/2)]

The smallest circle is at the middle, y = 0, with radius a = R |cos(φ/2)|; at the two bases r = R. Every point of all 4,040 pictures was checked against this formula. Because straight lines sweep out the whole surface, it is a ruled surface: a one sheet hyperboloid for a part turn, and a cone when the turn is exactly half way round and the bars meet on the axis.

The hyperbola that was spun

Put c = (L/2) |cot(φ/2)|. The radius equation rearranges into

r² / a² − y² / c² = 1

That is a hyperbola in a vertical plane, spun about the vertical y axis. The transverse axis runs sideways and meets the curve at r = ±a; the vertical axis is the other axis of symmetry and never meets it, exactly as the page says. When N is odd, no whole-number M gives exactly half a turn, so the closest setting leaves a tiny waist instead of a cone.

Press Hyperboloid, then drag the dot slowly to the right and watch the bright generator squeeze towards the middle before it opens out again.
